claim: Ptpn11 (Shp2) is a non-receptor tyrosine phosphatase that is an important transducer of growth factor and cytokine signals.
source: The non-receptor tyrosine phosphatase Ptpn11 (Shp2) is an important transducer of growth factor and cytokine signals.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature (Grossmann et al., 2010; Neel et al., 2003) in the introduction section.

claim: Loss of Ptpn11 drove muscle stem cells out of the proliferative state and into a resting state during postnatal muscle growth.
source: Loss of Ptpn11 drove muscle stem cells out of the proliferative and into a resting state during muscle growth.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Ptpn11 function in driving satellite cells into quiescence was observed in postnatal but not fetal myogenic stem cells.
source: This Ptpn11 function was observed in postnatal but not fetal myogenic stem cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data comparing fetal and postnatal timepoints.

claim: Muscle repair was severely perturbed when Ptpn11 was ablated in stem cells due to deficits in stem cell proliferation and survival.
source: Furthermore, muscle repair was severely perturbed when Ptpn11 was ablated in stem cells due to a deficit in stem cell proliferation and survival.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by regeneration experiments shown in the results.

claim: There is a molecular difference in the control of cell cycle withdrawal between fetal and postnatal myogenic stem cells.
source: Our data demonstrate a molecular difference in the control of cell cycle withdrawal in fetal and postnatal myogenic stem cells, and assign to Ptpn11 signaling a key function in satellite cell activity.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the differential requirement for Ptpn11 in fetal versus postnatal cells shown experimentally.

claim: Pax7+ progenitor cells give rise to primary fibers in embryos and permit growth of muscle mass during fetal and postnatal development as well as repair of injured muscle in adults.
source: The Pax7+ cells give rise to primary fibers in embryos, permit growth of muscle mass during fetal and postnatal muscle development as well as repair of injured muscle in the adult (Sambasivan et al., 2011; Lepper et al., 2011; McCarthy et al., 2011; Murphy et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Most Pax7+ cells reach quiescence when muscle fibers cease to grow by accretion of nuclei around P21 in mice.
source: Embryonic, fetal and postnatal Pax7+ cells proliferate, but most reach quiescence when muscle fibers cease to grow by accretion of nuclei (around P21 in mice; White et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to White et al., 2010.

claim: A small proportion of satellite cells remains in the cell cycle in adult sedentary mice and continues to contribute to fibers at a low and variable extent.
source: However, even in the muscle of adult sedentary mice, a small proportion of satellite cells remains in the cell cycle and continues to contribute to fibers, although to a low extent that is variable between muscles and animals (Chakkalakal et al., 2012; Keefe et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chakkalakal et al., 2012 and Keefe et al., 2015.

claim: Quiescence of adult stem cells allows their long-term survival and protects them from proliferative damage and cellular senescence.
source: Quiescence of adult stem cells allows their long-term survival and protects them from proliferative damage caused by mutations due to erroneous DNA replication, and from cellular senescence.
evidence: This is a general statement about stem cell biology supported by established knowledge.

claim: The tumor suppressor Rb has an important role in regulating quiescence, and its ablation results in increased muscle stem cells and accelerated cell cycle re-entry.
source: The tumor suppressor Rb has an important role in regulating quiescence and its ablation results in a vast increase of muscle stem cells and an accelerated cell cycle re-entry (Hosoyama et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hosoyama et al., 2011.

claim: Genetic ablation of Rbpj results in depletion of the quiescent satellite cell pool due to spontaneous activation and differentiation.
source: Genetic ablation of Rbpj encoding the transcription factor mediating canonical Notch signals results in a depletion of the quiescent satellite cell pool due to spontaneous activation and differentiation (Bjornson et al., 2012; Mourikis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bjornson et al., 2012 and Mourikis et al., 2012.

claim: Ablation of Sprouty 1 results in a mild elevation of the proportion of satellite cells that remain in the cell cycle.
source: In addition, ablation of Sprouty 1, an inhibitor of FGF signaling, results in a mild elevation of the proportion of satellite cells that remain in the cell cycle (Chakkalakal et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chakkalakal et al., 2012.

claim: Control of protein translation and phosphorylation of translation initiation factor eIF2α is essential for satellite cell quiescence.
source: Furthermore, control of protein translation and phosphorylation of translation initiation factor eIF2α is essential for quiescence (Zismanov et al., 2016; Crist et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zismanov et al., 2016 and Crist et al., 2012.

claim: Entry of satellite cells into quiescence in postnatal development depends on Hey1, Heyl, and the cell cycle inhibitor p27.
source: The mechanisms that allow satellite cells to enter quiescence in postnatal development are less well characterized but known to depend on Hey1 and Heyl, which might act downstream of Notch signals, as well as on the cell cycle inhibitor p27 (Fukada et al., 2011; Chakkalakal et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fukada et al., 2011 and Chakkalakal et al., 2014.

claim: Ptpn11 is an essential and positive mediator of signals provided by many receptors.
source: Ptpn11 (Shp2) is a tyrosine phosphatase that is an essential and positive mediator of signals provided by many receptors (Grossmann et al., 2010; Dance et al., 2008; Neel et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Grossmann et al., 2010, Dance et al., 2008, and Neel et al., 2003.

claim: Ptpn11 functions downstream of tyrosine kinase receptors are highly conserved in evolution and can be observed in invertebrates and vertebrates.
source: Functions of Ptpn11 downstream of tyrosine kinase receptors are highly conserved in evolution and can be observed in invertebrates and vertebrates (Perkins et al., 1992; Feng et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Perkins et al., 1992 and Feng et al., 1993.

claim: Ptpn11 frequently acts through regulation of Ras/Mapk/Erk1/2 signaling.
source: Ptpn11 frequently acts through regulation of Ras/Mapk/Erk1/2.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Ptpn11 is required to sustain but not to initiate Erk1/2 activity, indicating it mainly modulates feed-back regulation of the Ras/Mapk/Erk1/2 cascade.
source: In many cases, Ptpn11 is required to sustain but not to initiate Erk1/2 activity, indicating that it mainly modulates feed-back regulation of the Ras/Mapk/Erk1/2 branch of the signaling cascade (Grossmann et al., 2010; Dance et al., 2008; Neel et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Grossmann et al., 2010, Dance et al., 2008, and Neel et al., 2003.

claim: Ptpn11 was implicated in PI3K, Jak/Stat, Mapk/p38, NF-κB and NFAT signaling in a cell type- and receptor-specific manner.
source: In addition, Ptpn11 was implicated in PI3K, Jak/Stat, Mapk/p38, NF-κB and NFAT signaling in a cell type- and receptor-specific manner (reviewed in Grossmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Grossmann et al., 2010.

claim: Ptpn11 acts during migration of embryonic progenitor cells from somites into the limbs where it mediates signals provided by Met and its adaptor molecule Gab1.
source: In the context of myogenesis, Ptpn11 acts during migration of embryonic progenitor cells from somites into the limbs where it mediates signals provided by Met and its adaptor molecule Gab1 (Schaeper et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schaeper et al., 2007.

claim: Ptpn11 was assigned a role in hypertrophy as a regulator of NFAT activity.
source: In addition, Ptpn11 was assigned a role in hypertrophy as a regulator of NFAT activity (Fornaro et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fornaro et al., 2006.

claim: Pax7Cre efficiently recombined the Ptpn11 locus in myogenic progenitor cells.
source: Analysis of Ptpn11 protein by western blotting showed that it was present in stem cells isolated from fetal and postnatal muscle of control mice and strongly reduced in cells from coPtpn11 mutants (Figure 1a). Thus, Pax7Cre efficiently recombined the Ptpn11 locus.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1a demonstrating reduced Ptpn11 protein in mutant cells.

claim: coPtpn11 mutant mice displayed little change in muscle size at late fetal stages (E18) but severely compromised postnatal muscle growth.
source: We analyzed the consequences of the coPtpn11 mutation, and observed that mutant mice displayed little change in muscle size at late fetal stages (E18) but a severely compromised postnatal muscle growth (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The numbers of nuclei per fiber were reduced at P7 and P14 but little affected at P0 in coPtpn11 mutants compared to controls.
source: Compared to control mice, the numbers of nuclei per fiber were reduced at P7 and P14 but little affected at P0 (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The diameter of muscle fibers was unchanged at P0 but significantly reduced at P7 and P14 in coPtpn11 mutants compared to controls.
source: In accordance, the diameter of muscle fibers was unchanged at P0 (average fiber diameter 7.9 ± 0.5 μm and 7.9 ± 0.2 μm in control and coPtpn11 mutants, respectively) but significantly reduced at P7 (15.5 ± 0.1 μm and 12.5 ± 0.3 μm in control and coPtpn11 mutants, respectively) and P14 (18.2 ± 0.1 μm and 14.3 ± 0.3 μm in control and coPtpn11 mutants, respectively; see also Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by fiber diameter measurements and distribution data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: coPtpn11 mutant animals developed kyphosis by P14.
source: In addition, the animals developed kyphosis by P14 and therefore subsequent analyses were limited to P7 or earlier developmental stages.
evidence: This is an observed phenotype in the mutant animals.

claim: No significant difference in Pax7+ cell numbers was observed at E16, but at subsequent stages the number of Pax7+ cells declined drastically in coPtpn11 mice.
source: We observed no significant difference at E16 but at subsequent stages the number of Pax7+ cells declined drastically in coPtpn11 mice, which was confirmed by FACS (Figure 2a,b; Figure 2—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistology and FACS data shown in Figure 2a,b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: No difference in Pax7+ cell numbers was observed between Ptpn11flox/flox and Pax7Cre; Ptpn11flox/+ mice.
source: We also analyzed animals without a Pax7Cre allele (Ptpn11flox/flox) as additional control genotype, and observed no difference in Pax7+ cell numbers between Ptpn11flox/flox and Pax7Cre; Ptpn11flox/+ mice (Figure 2b; Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Ablation of Ptpn11 in myogenic progenitor cells has a severe effect on the size of the postnatal stem cell pool.
source: We conclude that ablation of Ptpn11 in myogenic progenitor cells has a severe effect on the size of the postnatal stem cell pool.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observed decline in Pax7+ cells in coPtpn11 mutants.

claim: BrdU incorporation and Ki67 expression in Pax7+ cells were similar in control and coPtpn11 mice at E16.5, but severely reduced in mutants at subsequent stages.
source: BrdU incorporation and Ki67 expression in Pax7+ cells were similar in control and coPtpn11 mice at E16.5, but at subsequent stages the numbers were severely reduced in mutants (Figure 2c–e).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistology and quantification data shown in Figure 2c-e.

claim: The downregulation of Ki67 in coPtpn11 mutant muscle stem cells indicates that they withdraw from the cell cycle prematurely.
source: Ki67 is expressed in proliferating cells in all stages of the cell cycle but not found in resting cells (Scholzen and Gerdes, 2000). The downregulation of Ki67 observed here indicates that the muscle stem cells withdraw from the cell cycle prematurely.
evidence: This interpretation is based on the known function of Ki67 as a proliferation marker and the observed downregulation in mutants.

claim: No change in apoptosis rates was observed by TUNEL staining in coPtpn11 mutants at P0.
source: No change in apoptosis rates was observed by TUNEL staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–e).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c-e.

claim: BrdU incorporation and Ki67 expression were compromised in cultured coPtpn11 mutant progenitors isolated from P0 but not from E14.5 mice.
source: BrdU incorporation and Ki67 expression were compromised in cultured coPtpn11 mutant progenitors isolated from P0 but not from E14.5 mice, and an intermediary effect was observed in E15.5 progenitors (Figure 2f–h).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification data from cultured cells shown in Figure 2f-h.

claim: Loss of Ptpn11 impairs proliferation in a cell-autonomous manner in postnatal but not fetal myogenic stem cells.
source: We conclude that loss of Ptpn11 impairs proliferation in a cell-autonomous manner. This Ptpn11 function is observed in stem cells of the postnatal but not fetal muscle.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the culture experiments showing differential effects at different developmental stages.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of Ptpn11 with GS493 in early postnatal mice severely reduced the number of Pax7+ cells that co-expressed Ki67 or incorporated BrdU.
source: When mice were treated for two days with the inhibitor, the number of Pax7+ cells that co-expressed Ki67 or incorporated BrdU was severely reduced (Figure 2i–l).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistology and quantification data shown in Figure 2i-l.

claim: No change in apoptosis rates was observed by TUNEL staining after GS493 treatment.
source: Similar to the conditional mutant mice, no change in apoptosis rates was observed by TUNEL staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f,g).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1f,g.

claim: In the absence of Ptpn11, early postnatal stem cells prematurely withdraw from the cell cycle.
source: We conclude that in the absence of Ptpn11, early postnatal stem cells prematurely withdraw from the cell cycle.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the genetic and pharmacological experiments showing reduced proliferation markers.

claim: Similar proportions of freshly FACS-isolated stem cells were Pax7- and MyoG-positive in control and coPtpn11 mutants, indicating that their differentiation propensity was unaffected.
source: Similar proportions of freshly FACS-isolated stem cells were Pax7- and MyoG-positive, regardless whether cells from control and coPtpn11 mutants or from control and GS493-treated mice were compared, indicating that their differentiation propensity was unaffected (Figure 3a–c).
evidence: This is supported by cytospin analysis and quantification shown in Figure 3a-c.

claim: FACS-isolated coPtpn11 mutant cells displayed no obvious fusion deficit when cultured in differentiation medium.
source: Furthermore, FACS-isolated coPtpn11 mutant cells displayed no obvious fusion deficit when cultured in differentiation medium (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining of differentiated cultures shown in Figure 3d.

claim: 752 differentially expressed genes were identified in neonatal stem cells from control and coPtpn11 mice (FC> ± 1.5; q < 0.05).
source: Next we performed gene expression profiling of neonatal stem cells from control and coPtpn11 mice. 752 differentially expressed genes were identified (FC> ± 1.5; q < 0.05; see Supplementary file 1 for the complete list of deregulated genes).
evidence: This is based on microarray analysis of FACS-isolated cells.

claim: GO term enrichment analysis demonstrated that down-regulated genes in coPtpn11 mutant cells encode components of various stages of the cell cycle.
source: GO term enrichment analysis demonstrated that down-regulated genes encode components of various stages of the cell cycle (e.g. G1/S-specific Ccne2; G1/S, S and M-specific Ranbp1; S, G2 and M phase specific Prc1; G2/M-phase specific Cdk1; M-phase-specific Ccnb1 and Nusap1; see also Supplementary file 1, 2).
evidence: This is based on GO term enrichment analysis of the microarray data.

claim: Four of the ten most strongly down-regulated genes in coPtpn11 mutant cells are known as immediate early genes that respond to growth factors (Egr4, Tnfrsf12a, Egr2, Plk2).
source: We also noted that among the ten most strongly down-regulated genes, four are known as immediate early genes that respond to growth factors (Egr4, Tnfrsf12a, Egr2, Plk2; Table 1; Supplementary file 1; Meighan-Mantha et al., 1999; Simmons et al., 1992; Müller et al., 1991; Gashler and Sukhatme, 1995).
evidence: This is based on microarray data shown in Table 1 and supported by citations.

claim: Many up-regulated genes in coPtpn11 mutant cells encode extracellular matrix proteins and proteases that remodel extracellular matrix (e.g. Col1a1/2, Col16a1, Adamts2).
source: Among the up-regulated genes, many encode extracellular matrix proteins and proteases that remodel extracellular matrix (e.g. Col1a1/2, Col16a1, Adamts2; Table 1; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on microarray data shown in Table 1.

claim: The downregulation of immediate early genes indicated that Ptpn11 mutant cells no longer respond appropriately to growth factor signaling.
source: Lastly, the observed downregulation of immediate early genes indicated that Ptpn11 mutant cells no longer respond appropriately to growth factor signaling.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the gene expression data.

claim: GS493 strongly inhibited Erk1/2 phosphorylation in C2C12 cells, but phosphorylation of Akt and p38 were unchanged.
source: GS493 strongly inhibited Erk1/2 phosphorylation (pErk1/2) and thus the activity of the Mapk/Erk1/2 pathway in C2C12 cells, but phosphorylation of Akt and p38 were unchanged (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Sustained pErk1/2 levels were severely decreased by GS493 in C2C12 cells after serum stimulation.
source: After starvation of C2C12 cells, addition of serum quickly up-regulated pErk1/2 in the presence or absence of the inhibitor. However, sustained pErk1/2 levels were severely decreased by GS493 (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot time course data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Downregulation of pErk1/2 levels was observed in isolated satellite cells from coPtpn11 mutant mice.
source: Downregulation of pErk1/2 levels was also observed in isolated satellite cells from coPtpn11 mutant mice (Figure 4c, quantified in d).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4c,d.

claim: Ptpn11 is required in myogenic cells for sustained activation of Mapk/Erk1/2.
source: Thus, Ptpn11 is required in myogenic cells for sustained activation of Mapk/Erk1/2.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the pharmacological and genetic experiments showing reduced sustained pErk1/2.

claim: qPCR analysis of Ptpn11 transcripts isolated from satellite cells of TxcoPtpn11 mice demonstrated efficient recombination after tamoxifen administration.
source: qPCR analysis of Ptpn11 transcripts isolated from satellite cells of TxcoPtpn11 mice demonstrated efficient recombination after tamoxifen administration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b,c).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b,c.

claim: pS6 and MyoD were present in satellite cells on fibers isolated from control and TxcoPtpn11 mice after 24 hrs of culture, whereas pErk1/2 staining was strongly reduced.
source: pS6 and MyoD were present in satellite cells on fibers isolated from control and TxcoPtpn11 mice after 24 hrs of culture, whereas pErk1/2 staining was strongly reduced (Figure 4e–g; Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 4e-g and Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claim: After 48 hrs, a substantial proportion of satellite cells from control and TxcoPtpn11 mice had entered the cell cycle and expressed Ki67.
source: After 48 hrs, a substantial proportion of satellite cells from control and TxcoPtpn11 mice had entered the cell cycle and expressed Ki67 (Figure 5a,b).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 5a,b.

claim: After 72 hrs, the majority of control satellite cells had undergone multiple cell divisions and formed small colonies, but satellite cells from TxcoPtpn11 mice divided rarely and had withdrawn from the cell cycle.
source: After 72 hrs, the majority of control satellite cells had undergone multiple cell divisions and formed small colonies, but satellite cells from TxcoPtpn11 mice divided rarely, most were BrdU-negative and had downregulated Ki67, indicating that they had withdrawn from the cell cycle (Figure 5c,d,f,g; Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 5c,d,f,g and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Map2k1DD expression rescued the deficits in colony size, BrdU incorporation and Ki67 expression in satellite cells that lack Ptpn11.
source: Cultured fibers from such animals demonstrated that Map2k1DD expression rescued the deficits in colony size, BrdU incorporation and Ki67 expression in satellite cells that lack Ptpn11 (Figure 5e–g).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 5e-g.

claim: Shp2 is a crucial regulator of Mapk/Erk1/2 activity in satellite cells.
source: We conclude from this experiment that Shp2 is a crucial regulator of Mapk/Erk1/2 activity in satellite cells.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the rescue experiment with constitutively active Map2k1.

claim: The proportion of MyoG expressing cells was increased when Ptpn11 was ablated in fiber culture.
source: We also noted that the proportion of MyoG expressing cells was increased when Ptpn11 was ablated, whereas sustained Mapk/Erk1/2 activity interfered with differentiation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,c,d).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,c,d.

claim: In myofiber culture, not only proliferation but also differentiation was affected by loss of Ptpn11.
source: Thus, in myofiber culture not only proliferation but also differentiation was affected by loss of Ptpn11.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observed increase in MyoG+ cells in fiber culture.

claim: A severe decline in satellite cell numbers was observed in TxcoPtpn11 mutants 90 days after introduction of the mutation, but numbers were not significantly changed 10 days after recombination.
source: A severe decline in satellite cell numbers was observed in TxcoPtpn11 mutants 90 days after introduction of the mutation, but numbers were not significantly changed 10 days after recombination (Figure 6a–c; Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistology and quantification data shown in Figure 6a-c and Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: The loss of satellite cells in TxcoPtpn11 mutants was slow and corresponded to a disappearance of 0.04 satellite cells/100 fibers/day when compared at P90.
source: Thus, the loss of cells observed was slow and corresponded to a disappearance of 0.04 satellite cells/100 fibers/day when TxcoPtpn11 and Txcontrol were compared at P90.
evidence: This is calculated from the quantification data.

claim: No elevated levels of apoptosis were observed in TxcoPtpn11 mutants using TUNEL or Caspase activity assays.
source: We did not observe elevated levels of apoptosis using TUNEL or Caspase activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c–f).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL staining and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1c-f.

claim: A significant downregulation of cell cycle markers (Ki67, Mcm2) was observed in TxcoPtpn11 mutant satellite cells.
source: However, a significant downregulation of cell cycle markers (Ki67, Mcm2) was observed.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Ptpn11 is essential for long-term maintenance of satellite cells in the adult.
source: Our data indicate that Ptpn11 is essential for long-term maintenance of satellite cells in the adult.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observed decline in satellite cells over 90 days.

claim: A significantly lowered number of Ki67+Pax7+ cells was observed in TxcoPtpn11 mutants compared to controls in sedentary muscle.
source: In accordance, we observed that Ki67 was expressed in a sub-population of Pax7+ cells in muscle of control sedentary mice, and noted a significantly lowered number of Ki67+Pax7+ cells in TxcoPtpn11 mutants (Figure 6e,f).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistology and quantification data shown in Figure 6e,f.

claim: Ablation of Ptpn11 drives the subpopulation of satellite cells that retain cell cycle activity into quiescence.
source: We conclude that ablation of Ptpn11 drives the subpopulation of satellite cells that retain cell cycle activity into quiescence, and also interferes with long term maintenance of satellite cells.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observed reduction in Ki67+ satellite cells.

claim: Regeneration of muscle was severely impaired in TxcoPtpn11 mutants seven days after injury.
source: Histological analyses indicated that regeneration of the muscle was severely impaired in TxcoPtpn11 mutants, and only few regenerated fibers with small diameter were discernable seven days after injury (Figure 7a–c).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis and fiber diameter measurements shown in Figure 7a-c.

claim: Fibrotic tissue and fat deposits had accumulated in TxcoPtpn11 mutants seven days after injury.
source: Instead, fibrotic tissue and fat deposits had accumulated (Figure 7d; Figure 7—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by Oil Red O staining and H&E staining shown in Figure 7d and Figure 7—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Increased numbers of C/EBPα+ adipocytes were observed in the damaged tissue of TxcoPtpn11 mutants seven days after injury.
source: Furthermore, seven days after injury increased numbers of C/EBPα+ adipocytes were observed in the damaged tissue of TxcoPtpn11 mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b,c; Cristancho and Lazar, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1b,c.

claim: Pax7+Vcam1+ satellite cells were rare in TxcoPtpn11 mice seven days after injury, whereas many were observed in control mice.
source: In accordance, we observed many Pax7+Vcam1+ cells in newly regenerated muscle of control mice, but in TxcoPtpn11 mice the Pax7+Vcam1+ satellite cells were rare (Figure 7e,f).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistology and quantification data shown in Figure 7e,f.

claim: Satellite cells require Ptpn11 to regenerate muscle tissue and to replenish the satellite cell pool.
source: Thus, satellite cells require Ptpn11 to regenerate muscle tissue and to replenish the satellite cell pool.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the impaired regeneration and reduced satellite cell numbers after injury.

claim: At 2.5 days after injury, the number of satellite cells was strongly reduced in TxcoPtpn11 mutant mice compared to control animals.
source: At 2.5 days after injury, the number of satellite cells was strongly reduced in TxcoPtpn11 mutant mice compared to control animals, and seven days after injury the number of satellite cells detected was even lower and had reached levels that were below the numbers present in uninjured muscle (Figure 7e,f).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7e,f.

claim: Apoptosis levels were increased 2.5 days after injury in TxcoPtpn11 mutants, indicating that satellite cells are lost due to apoptosis during this acute phase.
source: As assessed by TUNEL staining, apoptosis levels were increased 2.5 days after injury in TxcoPtpn11 mutants, indicating that during this acute phase satellite cells are lost due to apoptosis (Figure 7g).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL staining and quantification data shown in Figure 7g.

claim: Many satellite cells were Ki67+ 2.5 days after injury in TxcoPtpn11 mutants, but very few were positive for the M phase marker phospho-Histone H3.
source: This showed that many satellite cells were Ki67+, but very few were positive for the M phase marker phospho-Histone H3 (Figure 7h,i).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistology and quantification data shown in Figure 7h,i.

claim: In vivo Ptpn11 mutant satellite cells enter an early activation stage, but are unable to proliferate during regeneration.
source: We conclude that in vivo Ptpn11 mutant satellite cell enter an early activation stage, but are unable to proliferate, similarly to the changes observed in floating fiber culture.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the Ki67+ but pHH3- phenotype observed after injury.

claim: GS493 treatment seven days after injury severely reduced the proportion of Pax7+ cells that remained in the cell cycle and reduced the number of Pax7+ cells present in newly regenerated muscle.
source: GS493 severely reduced the proportion of Pax7+ cells that remained in the cell cycle and reduced the number of Pax7+ cells present in the newly regenerated muscle (Figure 8a–e).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistology and quantification data shown in Figure 8a-e.

claim: In the late phase of regeneration, GS493 neither induced increased apoptosis nor changed the proportion of cells expressing MyoG or C/EBPα.
source: In this late phase of the regeneration process, GS493 neither induced increased apoptosis nor did it change the proportion of cells expressing MyoG, or C/EBPα (Figure 8f,g; Figure 8—figure supplement 1a–e).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL staining, cytospin analysis, and quantification data shown in Figure 8f,g and Figure 8—figure supplement 1a-e.

claim: In the late phase of regeneration, satellite cells prematurely re-enter quiescence if Ptpn11 is inhibited.
source: We conclude that in the late phase of regeneration, satellite cells prematurely re-enter quiescence if Ptpn11 is inhibited.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the GS493 treatment experiments during late regeneration.

claim: Ptpn11 plays a central role in postnatal myogenesis of mice.
source: We demonstrate here that Ptpn11 plays a central role in myogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Patients with hypomorph mutations in Ptpn11 (Leopard or Noonan syndrome) display kyphosis, and functional muscle deficits might contribute to this phenotype.
source: It is interesting to note that patients with hypomorph mutations in Ptpn11 (Leopard or Noonan syndrome) also display kyphosis, and functional muscle deficits might contribute to the appearance of this phenotype (NIH-GARD, 2016a, 2016b).
evidence: This is a speculative connection between the mouse phenotype and human disease, supported by citations.

claim: Ptpn11 mainly acts by controlling sustained Mapk/Erk1/2 activity in myogenesis.
source: We combined complex genetic analyses, biochemical studies and pharmacological interference to show that Ptpn11 mainly acts by controlling sustained Mapk/Erk1/2 activity in myogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the mechanistic findings.

claim: The tyrosine phosphatase Ptpn11 is a central regulator of satellite cell activity during postnatal muscle growth and regeneration.
source: Our findings identify the tyrosine phosphatase Ptpn11 as a central regulator of satellite cell activity during postnatal muscle growth and regeneration.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Ptpn11 controls proliferation of postnatal but not fetal myogenic progenitor cells.
source: We show that Ptpn11 controls proliferation of postnatal but not fetal myogenic progenitor cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement of a key finding.

claim: A major switch exists in the signaling that controls proliferation during myogenesis.
source: Our data indicate that a major switch exists in the signaling that controls proliferation during myogenesis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differential Ptpn11 requirement at different developmental stages.

claim: Erk1/2 inhibition interferes with proliferation in fetal and adult myogenic cells.
source: Erk1/2 inhibition was previously described to interfere with proliferation in fetal and adult myogenic cells and, conversely, increasing Mapk/Erk1/2 activity by ablation of Sprouty1/2, enhances proliferation at both stages (Michailovici et al., 2014; Lagha et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Michailovici et al., 2014 and Lagha et al., 2008.

claim: Mapk/Erk1/2 but not Ptpn11 functions are stage-independent in myogenesis.
source: Thus, Mapk/Erk1/2 but not Ptpn11 functions are stage-independent.
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing the stage-specific requirement for Ptpn11 with the stage-independent role of Erk1/2.

claim: Growth of muscle and fiber diameter depends on accretion of nuclei.
source: Growth of muscle and fiber diameter also depends on accretion of nuclei, and we therefore suggest that the impairment is, to a large part, due to the observed stem cell deficit (White et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to White et al., 2010 and the observed correlation between reduced nuclei and reduced fiber diameter.

claim: Mutation of Ptpn11 in the muscle fiber results in a late-onset atrophy.
source: Mutation of Ptpn11 in the muscle fiber results in a late-onset atrophy (Fornaro et al., 2006; Princen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fornaro et al., 2006 and Princen et al., 2009.

claim: Atrophy might contribute to the deficit in muscle growth in coPtpn11 mutants since most nuclei in postnatal muscle fibers are expected to lack Ptpn11.
source: It is possible that atrophy might contribute to the deficit in muscle growth since most nuclei in the postnatal muscle fibers are expected to lack Ptpn11 in our model.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible contributing mechanism.

claim: Protein translation is repressed in quiescent satellite cells due to phosphorylation of the translation initiation factor eIF2α.
source: Protein translation is repressed in quiescent satellite cells due to phosphorylation of the translation initiation factor eIF2α (Zismanov et al., 2016; Crist et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zismanov et al., 2016 and Crist et al., 2012.

claim: The appearance of MyoD protein is a hallmark of satellite cell activation.
source: This repression is relieved when satellite cells get activated, and the appearance of MyoD protein is a hallmark of this.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about satellite cell activation.

claim: Ptpn11 signaling is dispensable for the entry into an early activation stage of satellite cells.
source: The appearance of MyoD indicates that Ptpn11 signaling is dispensable for the entry into an early activation stage.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that MyoD appears in Ptpn11 mutant cells.

claim: The proliferation deficit in Ptpn11 mutant satellite cells can be rescued by mild activation of the Mapk/Erk1/2 pathway.
source: It is interesting to note that the proliferation deficit can be rescued by a mild activation of the Mapk/Erk1/2 pathway, indicating that it is caused by impaired Mapk/Erk1/2 signaling.
evidence: This is based on the Map2k1DD rescue experiment.

claim: Ablation or inhibition of Ptpn11 in vivo drives Pax7+ cells into a resting state in postnatal development and at late stages of muscle regeneration.
source: We demonstrate here that ablation as well as short-term pharmacological inhibition of Ptpn11 in vivo drives Pax7+ cells into a resting state, and this is observed in postnatal development and at late stages of muscle regeneration.
evidence: This is a summary statement of findings from multiple experiments.

claim: The cell cycle exit of satellite cells in early postnatal or regenerating muscle after Ptpn11 inhibition/ablation is not accompanied by changes in the expression of differentiation markers in vivo.
source: Our data indicate that the cell cycle exit of satellite cells in early postnatal or regenerating muscle after Ptpn11 inhibition/ablation is not accompanied by changes in the expression of differentiation markers in vivo.
evidence: This is based on the observation that MyoG expression is unchanged in vivo.

claim: Pax7+ cells (re-)entered quiescence prematurely in postnatal development and muscle repair when Ptpn11 is absent or inhibited.
source: Thus, Pax7+ cells (re-)entered quiescence prematurely in postnatal development and muscle repair.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observed reduction in proliferation markers without increased differentiation.

claim: Ptpn11 mutation enhanced differentiation in satellite cells on cultured myofibers.
source: We did, however, note that Ptpn11 mutation enhanced differentiation in satellite cells on cultured myofibers.
evidence: This is based on the observed increase in MyoG+ cells in fiber culture.

claim: Differences in differentiation propensity can be observed in vivo and in vitro for Ptpn11 mutant satellite cells.
source: Thus, in regards to the effect on differentiation, differences can be observed in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: This is a comparison of the in vivo and in vitro observations.

claim: Satellite cells encounter distinct sets of growth factors in the in vivo environment and in culture, which may explain diverging differentiation propensity.
source: A possible explanation for the diverging differentiation propensity is that satellite cells encounter distinct sets of growth factors in the in vivo environment and in culture.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed differences.

claim: Ptpn11 controls entry into quiescence of emerging satellite cells in postnatal development.
source: We show here that Ptpn11 controls entry into quiescence of emerging satellite cells in postnatal development.
evidence: This is a summary statement of a key finding.

claim: Downregulation of sustained pErk activity suffices to drive postnatal stem cells out of the cell cycle.
source: Our data indicate that downregulation of sustained pErk activity suffices to drive these stem cells out of the cell cycle.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mechanistic findings.

claim: Hey/Heyl control entry into quiescence of satellite cells.
source: In addition to Ptpn11, the well-known target genes of Notch signaling, Hey/Heyl, control entry into quiescence, and sex hormones were recently noted to upregulate Notch signaling components and withdrawal of the cell cycle at puberty (Fukada et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fukada et al., 2011 and Kim et al., 2016.

claim: Sex hormones upregulate Notch signaling components and withdrawal of the cell cycle at puberty.
source: In addition to Ptpn11, the well-known target genes of Notch signaling, Hey/Heyl, control entry into quiescence, and sex hormones were recently noted to upregulate Notch signaling components and withdrawal of the cell cycle at puberty (Fukada et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fukada et al., 2011 and Kim et al., 2016.

claim: Ptpn11/Mapk/Erk1/2 and Notch signaling strengths may be modulated in the postnatal muscle and these signaling systems may interact to control entry into quiescence.
source: It is possible that Ptpn11/Mapk/Erk1/2 and Notch signaling strengths are modulated in the postnatal muscle and that these signaling systems interact to control entry into quiescence in emerging postnatal satellite cells.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible interactions between signaling pathways.
